To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) IPW estimators for the population effect of risk factors in a case-control study on a secondary outcome are inefficient relative to IPW estimators that additionally model the probability of disease, (2) the additional modeling assumption can be implemented in a semiparametric framework, (3) the efficient estimator in this class is a semiparamtric efficient estimator, and (4) the efficient estimator is more efficient than the IPW estimator in the unrestricted case, and more efficient

(1) we propose a new estimator for the effect of a risk factor on a secondary outcome that combines the inverse probability weighting estimator with a control function, which is an additional modeling assumption about the data generating process, and (2) we show that the new estimator is asymptotically more efficient than the standard inverse probability weighting estimator when the model for disease outcome is either parametric and semiparametric, and reduces to the standard estimator when the model is unrestricted.

1) the proposed estimators are regular, asymptotically linear, and consistent; 2) the proposed estimator is more efficient than the standard IPW estimator; and 3) the proposed estimator reduces to IPW when the disease outcome model is unrestricted, and the efficiency gains are greatest when the disease outcome probability is close to one or zero.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and evaluation of estimators for case-control studies with secondary outcomes.
improving the efficiency of IPW estimators in case-control studies, when the primary disease outcome probability model is specified.
the problem of estimating the effect of risk factor exposure on a secondary outcome when the data are collected via case-control sampling.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, in case-control studies where one is interested in estimating effects of risk factors on an outcome that is not the primary disease outcome, IPW is the preferred estimator when no additional assumptions are made about the disease outcome model, while IPW combined with a control function is preferred when additional assumptions are made.
our proposed control function assisted IPW estimators can be applied to case-control studies with a secondary outcome, and are efficient relative to standard IPW estimators.
our estimator is the most efficient estimator in the class of estimators that combine IPW and a control function.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the control function approach can be used to improve IPW estimators in case-control studies, and that it is especially useful when the primary disease outcome model is restricted.
we show that IPW is not always the optimal estimator in case-control studies, and that the optimal estimator is a control function assisted estimator, when the model for disease is restricted.
the efficiency of standard IPW estimators in case-control studies targeting secondary outcomes can be improved by incorporating additional information on the disease outcome probability.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the modeling assumptions required for efficient estimation of the effect of risk factor on a secondary outcome can be relaxed to the extent that the model for the disease outcome is correctly specified, without compromising efficiency.
, in case-control studies with a secondary outcome, IPW is inefficient, even when it is used in combination with correct specification of the primary outcome model.

, in case-control studies where the disease outcome is modeled, IPW is not the most efficient estimator for the effect of covariates on a secondary outcome, and that the additional modeling assumption of the disease outcome is useful.
